title: Diwali, festival of lights
hookLine: the festival of lights, kept by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, each for their own reasons
tomorrow: Buddhism: the man under the tree

lines: A CLAY LAMP THE SIZE OF A PALM.
cards: A clay lamp no bigger than a palm: a cotton wick, a spoon of oil. Now set one on every windowsill, every rooftop, every doorstep in a city. Colored powder patterns on the ground at the front door.
Sweets carried house to house in boxes. Fireworks cracking over the rooftops until late. New clothes.
Family on the phone from three continents. All of it on a night with no moon at all. Our Hindu visit ends with its festival of lamps: Diwali, the festival of lights.

teach.b: Diwali comes from the Sanskrit Deepavali, a row of lamps. It falls on a new moon night in autumn, and in many places the celebration runs over several days. But why light the lamps?
That depends on who you ask.

In much of north India, Hindus tell that Diwali remembers the god Rama coming home to his city, Ayodhya, after fourteen years of exile and his victory over the demon king Ravana, with the people lighting lamps to welcome him.
Hindu families also worship the goddess Lakshmi that night, asking her blessing on home and work. In parts of south India, the festival remembers Krishna's defeat of the demon Narakasura.
In Bengal, the same night belongs to the goddess Kali. And it isn't only Hindu.
Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, the day of release, remembering the sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, freed from imprisonment in Gwalior Fort, and the Golden Temple in Amritsar blazes with lights.

Jains remember the night Mahavira, in their tradition the twenty-fourth great teacher, attained final liberation; they light lamps because, as they tell it, the light of his wisdom had gone out of the world.
Same night, same lamps, different stories. Each tradition keeps its own, and none needs the others' to make sense.
What they share is the picture: light against the dark. And that closes our Hindu week. Dharma.
You are that. The act, not the fruit. Namaste.
Puja. And now, a row of lamps.

how: Hindu families light diyas, draw rangoli at the door, worship Lakshmi, share sweets and visit relatives; Sikhs light the Golden Temple for Bandi Chhor Divas; Jains mark Mahavira's liberation with lamps and prayer.

o: a spring festival of throwing colored powder at friends
a harvest festival thanking the gods for the year's crops
the festival of lights, from a word meaning a row of lamps

games.q: same night, own stories — tap the pairs.

s: Diwali is only a Hindu festival
Sikhs keep Bandi Chhor Divas and Jains mark Mahavira's liberation on the same night.
Diwali falls on a new moon night
a night with no moon, in autumn.
every Hindu tells the same Diwali story
Rama's return, Lakshmi, Krishna and Narakasura, Kali: it depends on the region and family.

games.q: it's the darkest night of the month, with no moon at all. you're in Ayodhya and your exiled prince is coming home. what do you do?
o: wait until morning to greet him.
line every window and doorstep with lamps.
light one fire in the square.
games.why: in the story many Hindus tell, the people lit rows of lamps to welcome Rama home, and Diwali still fills the dark with them.

practice: If it's safe, set a candle or a small light where it can be seen from outside; if not, picture a single clay lamp on a windowsill at night. Think of one darkness near you: a worry, a grief, someone having a hard month.
Don't fix it; just let the small flame sit beside it.

wordCard.voice: Diwali. The festival of lights: a row of lamps kept by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains on the same night, each for their own reasons. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a row of lamps, the older form of Diwali.
